articles.title: Open-weight models narrow the gap on closed labs
articles.subtitle: New benchmarks show small open models closing in on frontier scale.
content: This week's releases confirm a trend that has been building for months: openly licensed weights now trail the largest closed models by a single-digit margin on standard reasoning benchmarks.
Cost curves tell part of the story. Training runs that once required thousands of accelerators are being replicated on smaller, rented clusters, and several teams shared reproducible recipes.
The practical takeaway for builders is a shift in default advice: many products no longer need a frontier API at all.

articles.title: A post-quantum migration checklist lands for libraries
articles.subtitle: Dependency maintainers now have a concrete path to PQC readiness.
content: A widely-used cryptography library published its migration guide this week, giving maintainers a phased plan that starts with audit tooling rather than key-swapping.
The guide stresses that algorithm agility in protocol design matters more than any single new primitive.

articles.title: Edge caching becomes the default, not the hack
articles.subtitle: Platforms are folding regional replication into their base tier.
content: Two major hosting platforms quietly made edge replication part of their default pricing this month, a shift that removes a whole class of latency hacks.
Developers on the old model had to reason about cache invalidation as a feature; now the platform handles the plumbing.

articles.title: A weekend experiment becomes a company's main pipeline
articles.subtitle: A hobby script quietly grew into production infrastructure.
content: It started as a 40-line script in a developer's weekend log and ended as the ingestion path for three products.
The lesson, the team says, was keeping the interfaces boring and the internals replaceable.

articles.title: Retrieval pipelines get honest about rerankers
articles.subtitle: Teams are reporting that rerankers add less than their latency suggests.
content: A new evaluation compares two-stage retrieval against a single well-tuned retriever and finds the reranker gains are thin once the first stage is already strong.
The takeaway: measure before you add a stage, and treat reranking as a tuned optimization rather than a default.

articles.title: Smaller context budgets are back in fashion
articles.subtitle: Agents that trim their context window are getting cheaper and faster.
content: Several agent frameworks now ship context-compaction passes that summarize old turns instead of replaying them.
Benchmarks show only modest quality loss at a fraction of the token cost.

articles.title: Fine-tuning datasets finally come with provenance
articles.subtitle: The 'garbage in, garbage out' problem gets a ledger.
content: New dataset formats embed licensing and lineage metadata by default, so teams can audit what went into a checkpoint.
It is a small convention change with an outsized effect on reproducibility.

articles.title: Command-line tools get a second life as defaults
articles.subtitle: Terminal utilities are quietly winning the adoption war again.
content: Every few years the industry rediscovers that small, composable command-line tools outlive their GUI replacements.
This cycle the winners are the ones with honest help output and no config file.

articles.title: A 4 a.m. deploy, a daylight-savings bug, and a lesson
articles.subtitle: The story that keeps reminding us to test for clocks.
content: A service that had run flawlessly for two years broke at 4 a.m. because it assumed a UTC offset would never change.
The postmortem is a small classic of the genre, and its conclusion is still the right one: store instants, display zones.

articles.title: Daily DSA Question
articles.subtitle: Difficulty: medium
content: Given an array of integers, return the length of the longest increasing subsequence.
Aim for O(n log n) using a patience-sorting approach, then explain why binary search is valid there.

articles.title: Today's Comic
articles.subtitle: The continuing strip
content: Panel three: the engineer removes the 'it works on my machine' sticky note, revealing the fine print: 'and nowhere else.'
